newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST - Iberian short bond yields seen easing.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Iberian short bond yields seen easing.

text.p: Yields on bonds with maturities of up to three years are expected to ease in Iberia over the next week in anticipation of further Spanish and Portuguese official rate cuts soon, analysts said.

"December 1996 inflation figures should lead markets to expect further Spanish and Portuguese rate cuts, and this will increase investors' interest in the short end of the yield curve," said Serge Goncalves of FINMAT in London.
"In Spain and Portugal, the betting is on maturities of up to three years, where there will be a bigger drop in yields," said an analyst with an investment bank in London.
"Except for 10-year bonds, there could be some arbitrage between Portuguese bonds and Bonos," he added.

October 1999 Bonos are yielding 5.43 percent to give a spread of 36 basis points (bps) below April 2001 Bonos, which yield 5.79 percent. April 2001 Bonos are 108 bps below April 2006 Bonos, which yield 6.87 percent.
March 1999 Portuguese bonds (OTs) are yielding 5.66 percent, 23 bps above October 1999 Bonos, while March 2001 Portuguese bonds yield 5.97 percent, 18 bps more than April 2001 Bonos.

"In the coming week, October 1999 Bonos could ease to 5.30 percent. The yield spread between three-year Portuguese bonds and Bonos could drop to 10 bps and between five-year maturities could remain almost flat," FINMAT's Goncalves said.
"For maturities of up to five years it is logical by buy Portuguese bonds by selling Bonos," he added.

"Portugal is better placed than Spain to enter European Monetary Union from the start in 1999. "But Portuguese bonds of up to five years have very large positive spreads against Bonos, which are not justified."

Analysts said they expected December inflation data, due on January 14 or 15 in Portugal and January 15 in Spain, to raise the possibility of official rate cuts in February, which will lead to lower short bond yields, steepening the yield curve.

"The spread between three and five year bonds could increase by five to eight bps," said Henrik Lumholdt, an analyst with Bank of America in Madrid. "There will be no changes in maturities between five and 10 years," he said.
Analysts expected spreads between 10-year Iberian bonds and Bunds to stay steady around 100 bps over the next week.

After the tightening of spreads between 10-year bonds and Bunds in 1996, Iberian investors want to take refuge in shorter bonds to avoid the volatility of longer bonds which stems from the release of economic data in "core" markets, they said.
"I think a lot of people are worried that there is only a little bit of easing left (in spreads between 10-year Bonos and Bunds)", said Luca Jellenick of Banque Paribas in London.
"If we look at the recent auctions of Bonos, we see that people are more interested in buying shorter bonds," he added.

Debby Bennellick, analyst at UBS in London, said "I think that in February there could be a cut of 25 bps in the Spanish repo rate (to 6.0 percent) and a cut of 30 to 40 bps in the Portuguese repo rate (to 6.4 or 6.3 percent)."
Lumholdt said the Bank of Spain could cut its repo rate, perhaps in February, by 25 to 50 basis points.
Isabel Cabral of Lisbon broker Fincor said: "I would say that the Bank of Portugal could cut its repo rate by 20 to 30 bps, probably in February, but perhaps in January."
Analysts said the recent strengthening of the escudo against the mark boosted arguments for an official rate cut in Iberia.
In November prices were unchanged in Spain to give year-on-year inflation of 3.2 percent. In Portugal prices rose by 0.2 percent to give a year-on-year figure of 3.0 percent.
"In Spain...December inflation...could be 0.3 percent to give the same year-on-year figure of 3.2 percent," said Lumholdt.
Cabral said "I expect inflation in December in Portugal to be unchanged to give a year-on-year rate of 3.2 percent."
